guidingQuestion: How do producers capture energy and matter?
hook: A giant sequoia starts as a seed lighter than a paperclip and grows into one of the most massive living things on Earth, so where did all that wood come from?

sections.title: Key Science Concept: Matter and Energy in Photosynthesis
5. Biomass Is a Source of Energy for Humans

objectives.text: Identify producers on land and in water and the cell structures (chloroplasts) where most of them capture light. Tell the energy input of photosynthesis (light) apart from its matter inputs (carbon dioxide and water).

Use the balanced photosynthesis equation to explain how the atoms of carbon dioxide and water are rearranged into sugar and oxygen, with no atoms gained or lost, while light energy ends up stored as chemical energy.
sections: Key Science Concept: Matter and Energy in Photosynthesis

objectives.text: Draw on experimental evidence to explain where a plant's matter comes from, and predict how a change in light or carbon dioxide affects a producer's ability to make food.
Explain how producers use sugar right away, store it as starch, or build it into cellulose, and how that stored matter and energy (biomass) reaches the organisms that eat them.
Evaluate fuel choices for jets using engineering criteria and constraints, such as energy per kilogram, renewability, cost, and competition with food crops.
sections: 5. Biomass Is a Source of Energy for Humans

keyIdeas: Producers make their own food. They include plants, algae such as diatoms and Volvox, and cyanobacteria, and nearly every other living thing depends on the food they make.

Photosynthesis takes in one energy input, light, and two matter inputs, carbon dioxide and water. In plants and algae it happens in chloroplasts, where the green pigment chlorophyll absorbs the light.
The balanced equation 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ shows atoms being rearranged: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen atoms on each side, none created or destroyed.
Light is energy, not matter. It never becomes atoms of sugar. Its energy ends up stored as chemical energy in the sugar, which a cell can release later when the sugar reacts with oxygen.

Experiments built this explanation. Ingenhousz found that green plant parts give off oxygen only in light, and Saussure's sealed jars showed that most of a plant's matter comes from carbon dioxide in the air, not from soil.
Producers break some sugar down right away for energy, store some as starch in roots, seeds and fruits, and link sugar units into cellulose to build stiff cell walls.
Biomass is the matter of living things, and it holds stored energy. When animals eat producers, that matter and energy become part of the animals.
Engineers judge biofuels against criteria, like lots of energy per kilogram, and constraints, like being renewable and not crowding out food crops. Burning any biofuel still releases carbon dioxide.

glossary.definition: Anything that takes up space and has mass, from a grain of sand to the air in your lungs.
An organism that makes its own food from simple materials in its surroundings, usually by capturing light energy.
Tiny producers, such as diatoms, that drift in the sunlit upper waters of oceans and lakes.
The chemical reaction producers use to build sugar and give off oxygen from carbon dioxide and water, powered by light energy.
A small green structure inside plant and algae cells where photosynthesis takes place.
The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy to power photosynthesis.
A substance that goes into a chemical reaction, written before the arrow in an equation.
A substance made by a chemical reaction, written after the arrow in an equation.
A storage molecule made of many sugar units linked together, packed into roots, seeds and fruits for later use.
Long chains of linked sugar units that form the stiff walls of plant cells. It is the largest single ingredient of wood, and cotton is nearly pure cellulose.
The total mass of living things or their remains, which holds both matter and stored chemical energy.
A fuel made from biomass, such as plant waste, that releases energy when it burns.
A goal a design should meet as well as possible, such as packing lots of energy into each kilogram of fuel. The plural is criteria.
A limit a design must stay within, such as a fuel having to come from a renewable resource or stay affordable.

explorer.title: Meet the Sun-Catchers
paragraphs: Every food chain needs a starting point: an organism that makes its own food instead of eating it. These producers are everywhere. On land, trees, grasses, ferns and mosses do the job. In water, eelgrass grows in shallow bays, while algae such as Volvox colonies and drifting diatoms do most of the work. Cyanobacteria, tiny single-celled producers, turn up in almost every habitat on Earth.

Zoom into a leaf and you find cells. Inside its food-making cells sit many chloroplasts, the small structures where photosynthesis happens. Chloroplasts are packed with chlorophyll, a green pigment that absorbs light energy.

Photosynthesis has one energy input and two matter inputs. Light, usually sunlight, supplies the energy. Carbon dioxide from the air (or dissolved in water) and water from the soil or surroundings supply the atoms. Take away any one of the three, and a producer cannot make food.

diagram.caption: Some producers from this lesson
diagram.alt: A table of six producers. Pine or maple tree: lives on land; is a plant. Moss or fern: lives on land; is a plant. Eelgrass: lives in shallow bays and other waters; is a plant. Volvox: lives in fresh water; not a plant, it is a colony of single-celled green algae. Diatom: lives in the sunlit top layer of the ocean; not a plant, it is a single-celled alga (phytoplankton). Cyanobacteria: live almost everywhere on land and in water; not plants, they are single-celled bacteria.
rows: No: a colony of single-celled green algae
Sunlit top layer of the ocean

explorer.watchOut: Producers are not only plants: algae and cyanobacteria count too. And leaves look green because chlorophyll absorbs green light more weakly than red or blue light, not because it absorbs none. A typical leaf still captures most of the green light that hits it.

explorer.title: Atoms Change Partners
paragraphs: Photosynthesis is a chemical reaction, and chemists write it as a balanced equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Before the arrow are the reactants, carbon dioxide and water. After the arrow are the products, sugar (glucose) and oxygen gas.

A coefficient, the big number in front of a formula, counts molecules. A subscript, the small number inside a formula, counts atoms of one element in a single molecule. So 6CO₂ means six carbon dioxide molecules, each with one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.

Count every atom and you find 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen atoms on each side. Nothing is created or destroyed; atoms leave their old partners and join new ones. That is why six carbon dioxide molecules are needed for each sugar molecule: sugar holds six carbon atoms, and each carbon dioxide brings one.

Light appears in the equation as energy, not as a substance. It drives the rearranging, and the energy ends up stored as chemical energy in the sugar, ready to be released later when the sugar reacts with oxygen inside a cell.

diagram.caption: The balanced equation for photosynthesis
diagram.alt: Six molecules of carbon dioxide, C O 2, plus six molecules of water, H 2 O, with light energy shown over the arrow, produce one molecule of sugar, C 6 H 12 O 6, plus six molecules of oxygen gas, O 2. Each side has 6 carbon atoms, 12 hydrogen atoms and 18 oxygen atoms.

explorer.watchOut: Books often say energy is "stored in the bonds" of sugar. That is handy shorthand, but breaking a bond actually takes energy. Energy is released when sugar reacts with oxygen and new, more stable bonds form in carbon dioxide and water. Also remember that sunlight never turns into atoms.

explorer.title: Detectives of the Greenhouse
paragraphs: Where does a giant sequoia's matter come from? Scientists have chased that question for centuries, and they answered it with experiments rather than guesses.

In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz put green leaves into clear jars of water and set them in sunshine. Bubbles of gas gathered on the leaves. After sunset, hardly any formed, and leaves kept in shade gave off poorer air. The gas from sunlit leaves turned out to be rich in oxygen. Because the results changed with light, he could link the oxygen to light.

Notice the two kinds of statements. The bubbles he saw and the gas he tested were observations: things seen or measured. "Light makes green leaves give off oxygen" was his conclusion: an explanation built by comparing those observations.

In the early 1800s, Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure sealed plants in jars so he could track how much carbon dioxide they took in. His evidence showed that most of a plant's matter comes from carbon dioxide in the air, with water supplying a smaller share. Soil adds only a little, in the form of minerals.

You can use the same reasoning to predict. Take away light and photosynthesis stops. Use up the carbon dioxide and sugar-making stalls, even under a bright lamp. Leave a plant in the dark and it survives for a while on food it stored earlier.

diagram.caption: Two experiments that explained how plants get matter
diagram.alt: A table of two experiments. Jan Ingenhousz, late 1700s: asked how plants use or give off gases; put green leaves in jars of water, compared leaves in sunlight with leaves in shade or after sunset, and collected the gas bubbles; found that green plant parts give off oxygen only in light. Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure, early 1800s: asked where most of a plant's mass comes from; sealed plants in jars and tracked the carbon dioxide they used; found that most of a plant's matter comes from carbon dioxide, with water supplying a smaller share.
rows: How do plants use or give off gases?
Leaves in jars of water, in sunlight versus shade or night; gas bubbles collected
Green parts give off oxygen only in light
Where does most of a plant's mass come from?
Carbon dioxide used by plants sealed in jars
Most of a plant's matter comes from carbon dioxide; water supplies a smaller share

explorer.watchOut: The textbook's drawing of Ingenhousz's jars shows a plant giving off carbon dioxide in the dark. That does not mean plants break down sugar only at night. Plant cells use sugar for energy day and night; in bright light, photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide faster than that process gives it off. Also, the "oxygen bubbles" in that drawing are symbols: gas bubbles you can see form only on plants under water.

explorer.title: Sugar's Three Jobs
paragraphs: A producer does three things with the sugar it makes. It breaks some down right away to release energy for its cells' work. It stores some, often as starch, in roots, seeds and fruits. And it links sugar units into cellulose, the stiff material of plant cell walls.

Storage matters because light does not last. At night, on cloudy days, or inside a buried seed, a plant lives on food it packed away earlier. That is why carrots and beets taste sweet, and why a seed can sprout before it has any leaves.

All the matter of living things is called biomass, and most of Earth's biomass belongs to producers. When an animal eats a plant, it takes in that matter and its stored energy and turns some of it into its own body. Some of the carbon in a slice of wheat bread was floating in the air as carbon dioxide not long ago.
Over billions of years, photosynthesis also filled the air with oxygen. Without it, Earth's land would likely be bare rock and dust, and life as we know it could not exist.

diagram.caption: Where a producer's sugar goes (arrows show matter moving)
diagram.alt: Five boxes joined by arrows. Carbon dioxide and water point to sugar made in leaves, labeled photosynthesis. Sugar points to starch stored in roots and seeds, labeled stored. Sugar points to cellulose in cell walls, labeled built. Sugar points back to carbon dioxide and water, labeled broken down for energy. Starch points to an animal that eats the plant, labeled eaten.

explorer.watchOut: Cellulose is not whole sugar molecules glued end to end: each link leaves out the atoms of one water molecule. And "all life depends on photosynthesis" is nearly right but not quite: some communities, such as those around deep-sea vents and seeps, run on chemical energy instead of sunlight.

explorer.title: Fuel for Flight
paragraphs: A jet burns fuel to release stored chemical energy. Engineers want a fuel that packs as much energy as possible into each kilogram, because every extra kilogram of fuel is more mass the jet has to lift. That goal is a criterion, a measure of how well a solution works.

Starting in the 2000s, airlines added a constraint, a limit any solution must respect: the fuel should come from renewable resources. Fossil fuels fail that test. Biofuels, made from biomass such as plant material, can pass it.

Not all biomass works equally well. Cutting slow-growing trees is not renewable on a useful timescale, and crops grown for fuel can push out food crops and raise prices. The textbook's engineers favored city waste such as grass clippings, food scraps and cardboard: a steady supply of cellulose that might otherwise go to a landfill.

Biofuels are not magic. Burning them still releases carbon dioxide; their advantage is that their carbon was pulled from the air by producers recently, and the supply can be renewed. Real aviation biofuels are refined into fuels that behave like ordinary jet fuel. As of 2026, aviation biofuels cost several times more than ordinary jet fuel and are expected to make up under 1 percent of jet fuel use (IATA).

diagram.caption: Checking fuel sources against the textbook's constraints
diagram.alt: A table comparing four fuel sources on two questions. Fossil jet fuel: not renewable; does not compete with food crops. Biofuel from slow-growing trees: renewable only if trees are regrown fast enough; does not compete with food crops. Biofuel from food crops on farmland: renewable; does compete with food crops and can raise food prices. Biofuel from city waste: renewable, with a steady new supply; does not compete with food crops.
rows: Biofuel from food crops on farmland
Yes, and can raise food prices

explorer.watchOut: Renewable does not mean unlimited or carbon-free. A renewable source lasts only if it is used no faster than it is replaced, and burning any biofuel releases carbon dioxide.

reviewFlags.resolution: Pages 42, 47 and 48 were rendered and read (Figure 2B also at 220 dpi). The equation is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, balanced with 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side, and the p. 48 art labels 6CO₂, 6H₂O, C₆H₁₂O₆ and 6O₂. Content uses 'chemical equation' for the whole reaction and 'formula' for each substance.

evidence.supports: The chemical equation for photosynthesis is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, with reactants on the left and products on the right.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept: Matter and Energy in Photosynthesis (rendered)
evidence.supports: Carbon dioxide and water are used and sugar and oxygen are produced, with energy from sunlight driving the reaction.

reviewFlags.issue: The lesson repeatedly says the Sun's energy is 'stored in chemical bonds' of sugar (pp. 43, 46, 47, 48, 50, 53) and that cells 'release the energy stored in the bonds' (p. 50). This is common shorthand (OpenStax uses it too), but taken literally it suggests that breaking bonds releases energy, which the brief's guardrail rules out: breaking bonds requires energy and forming bonds releases it.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says light energy ends up stored as chemical energy in the sugar and is released when the sugar reacts with oxygen. It never says breaking a bond releases energy. The O2 Science Explorer watchOut explains the shorthand. No question asks where in the molecule the energy sits. L04-Q12 asks what happens to absorbed light energy and keys 'stored as chemical energy in the sugar' and 'released when the sugar reacts with oxygen', never bond breaking.

evidence.locator: Section 2. Producers Use Photosynthesis, Light Causes a Chemical Reaction
evidence.supports: Photosynthesis needs an input of energy, which is transferred to the products and stored in the sugar.

evidence.title: Chemical energetics: words matter
evidence.supports: Students often wrongly believe breaking bonds releases stored energy; energy changes make sense only when the whole reaction, including the oxygen reactant and the bonds formed in the products, is considered.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 8.1 Overview of Photosynthesis
evidence.supports: Introductory biology texts commonly describe the captured energy as stored in the covalent bonds of sugar; six carbon dioxide and six water molecules produce one sugar and six oxygen molecules.

reviewFlags.issue: Page 46 says chlorophyll does not absorb green light and 'reflects mostly green light'. Leaves do absorb green light, just less strongly than red or blue: a typical leaf absorbs about 90 percent of red and blue light and about 70 to 80 percent of green light, and absorbed green light drives photosynthesis.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says chlorophyll absorbs green light weakly, so more green light leaves the leaf. L04-Q07 is keyed to 'absorbs less green than red or blue'. L04-Q08 asks learners to predict that a green-lit leaf still makes some sugar in a short test, carries the external record, and tells learners that the textbook's 'does not absorb green light' is a simplification. No question says chlorophyll absorbs no green light.

evidence.locator: Section 2. Producers Use Photosynthesis, Chlorophyll Absorbs Energy from Light
evidence.supports: Chlorophyll absorbs only certain colors of light, and the light that leaves the leaf makes it look green.

evidence.title: Why are leaves green?
evidence.publisher: The University of Tokyo (feature by Ichiro Terashima)
evidence.supports: An ordinary leaf absorbs around 90 percent of red and blue light and around 70 to 80 percent of green light; once absorbed, green light drives photosynthesis about as well as red light.

reviewFlags.issue: The Figure 3 labels (p. 49) say plants in sunlight give off oxygen and take in carbon dioxide, while plants in the dark give off carbon dioxide. Read alone, this suggests plants use sugar for energy only in the dark. The brief's guardrail says plants photosynthesize and respire.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content and L04-Q15 teach that plant cells break down sugar for energy day and night; in bright light photosynthesis outpaces it, so the plant gives off oxygen overall. The O3 card's watchOut names the mix-up. Page 50 supports the point that producers' own cells release the energy in sugar.

evidence.supports: In sunlight the plants gave off oxygen bubbles and took in carbon dioxide; in the dark they gave off carbon dioxide and no oxygen bubbles.

evidence.locator: Section 4. Storing Energy and Matter, Stored Energy and Matter in Organisms
evidence.supports: Producers' cells carry out reactions that release the energy stored in sugar to survive, grow and reproduce.

evidence.title: Plant resistance to stress: role of respiration?
evidence.publisher: Encyclopedia of the Environment (Pierre Dizengremel, Université de Lorraine)
evidence.supports: Plant respiration takes place day and night, unlike photosynthesis; respiration also continues in the light, though more weakly.

evidence.title: Botany online: Photosynthesis
evidence.supports: Ingenhousz recognized the role of light, and plants take up small amounts of oxygen and give off carbon dioxide at night or in shade.

reviewFlags.issue: Page 49 says Saussure's evidence showed plants get 'about 70 percent' of their matter from carbon dioxide and most of the rest from water. Modern estimates of a plant's dry mass are higher for the air: about 45 percent carbon and 45 percent oxygen that trace back to carbon dioxide, about 6 percent hydrogen from water, and about 4 percent soil minerals. The exact share depends on whether water in living tissue is counted.
reviewFlags.resolution: No question tests the 70 percent figure. Questions say 'most' of a plant's dry mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air, with water supplying a smaller share and soil only a few percent (L04-Q16 defines dry mass in its conditions). This matches the brief: soil does not supply most plant mass.

evidence.supports: Saussure sealed plants in jars to track the carbon dioxide they used and found that most of a plant's matter comes from carbon dioxide, with much of the rest from water.

evidence.title: Plants Lesson 3 Background Information
evidence.supports: A plant's dry mass is carbon-based and its carbon comes from carbon dioxide in the air, not soil or water; roughly 45 percent carbon and 45 percent oxygen from air, about 6 percent hydrogen from water, about 4 percent soil minerals.

evidence.title: Botany online: Photosynthesis
evidence.supports: Van Helmont's potted willow gained a great deal of weight while its soil lost only about two ounces; Saussure showed that the weight gain also depends on binding the components of water, not only carbon and minerals.

reviewFlags.issue: Page 51 says 'all other organisms' get their energy ultimately from producers through photosynthesis, and that the living parts of Earth's ecosystems would have no other way of accessing matter or energy. Page 43 more carefully says 'nearly all'. Deep-sea vent and seep communities are based on chemosynthesis, which runs on chemical energy instead of sunlight.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says 'nearly all' life depends on photosynthesis, and the O4 card's watchOut names the vent and seep exception. No question asks learners to agree that every organism depends on photosynthesis. L04-Q23 asks about a single grassland food chain, which does start with photosynthesis.

evidence.supports: Photosynthesis is the source of nearly all the energy and matter used by other organisms on Earth.

evidence.title: What is the difference between photosynthesis and chemosynthesis?
evidence.supports: Photosynthesis is powered by sunlight while chemosynthesis runs on chemical energy; chemosynthesis supports communities at hydrothermal vents and cold seeps, and together the two fuel all life on Earth.

reviewFlags.issue: Page 45 says some cyanobacteria live in hot springs 'that have boiling-hot temperatures'. Photosynthetic cyanobacteria stop growing at about 70 to 74 °C; the hottest, near-boiling springs are home to other heat-loving bacteria and archaea, not producers that use light.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content does not repeat the hot-spring claim, and no question tests the temperature.

evidence.locator: Section 1. Producers Capture Energy and Matter, Producers in Aquatic Ecosystems
evidence.supports: Cyanobacteria are single-celled producers found in many aquatic ecosystems, from frozen lakes to hot springs.

evidence.title: Thermophilic microbes: Yellowstone National Park (The Microbial World)
evidence.supports: The upper temperature limit for growth of cyanobacteria is 70 to 74 °C, while other microorganisms occupy water up to about 100 °C.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 5 (pp. 52-53) is dated and simplified. It says biofuels give airlines a 'low-cost' source of fuel and that the sugars are made into 'alcohol that is used as fuel'. As of 2026 (IATA, about 0.8 percent expected), aviation biofuel (sustainable aviation fuel) costs several times more than conventional jet fuel and is expected to be under 1 percent of jet fuel use; alcohols must be converted into jet-fuel hydrocarbons and blended (alcohol-to-jet), and many current fuels come from waste fats and oils. The text also calls high energy per unit mass 'efficient', where engineers would say energy per kilogram (specific energy).
reviewFlags.resolution: Questions treat the city-waste strategy as the textbook's design example (L04-Q26's prompt calls it the textbook's design story, and its landfill reason keeps the textbook's hedge, 'might go to landfills'; the O5 card says 'might otherwise go to a landfill') and test the reasoning (criteria, constraints, trade-offs), not cost or market claims. L04-Q26 carries a dated limitation (as of 2026, IATA) with cost and share, and the O5 card gives the same dated figures. Content uses 'energy per kilogram'. The O5 card adds that biofuels still release carbon dioxide.

evidence.locator: Section 5. Biomass Is a Source of Energy for Humans, Constraints Help Identify the Best Source of Biomass
evidence.supports: The textbook presents city waste as a renewable, low-cost biofuel source that still releases carbon dioxide when burned.

evidence.title: Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)
evidence.supports: As of 2026 (IATA, about 0.8 percent expected), SAF is several times more expensive than conventional aviation fuel and makes up less than 1 percent of global aviation fuel use; burning it produces exhaust similar to fossil jet fuel.

evidence.title: Alternative Fuels Data Center: Sustainable Aviation Fuel
evidence.supports: SAF is made from feedstocks such as woody biomass, fats and oils, and food and yard waste; approved pathways include alcohol-to-jet, which converts alcohols into jet fuel, and blends are limited to 10 to 50 percent.

evidence.title: Sustainable Aviation Fuels
evidence.publisher: U.S. Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office
evidence.supports: SAF technologies break down biomass and waste resources and recombine them into energy-dense hydrocarbons.

reviewFlags.issue: Page 50 says cellulose 'looks like many sugar molecules bound together'. Cellulose is a chain of linked glucose units, but each link leaves out the atoms of one water molecule (each unit is glucose minus H₂O), so the chain is not whole sugar molecules glued together.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content calls cellulose and starch chains of linked sugar units. The O4 watchOut and the L04-Q21 explanation say each link leaves out the atoms of one water molecule. That wording states the composition only; it does not claim how the cell forms the link (the classroom 'dehydration' model, in which water is given off, is not how plant cells actually build cellulose). No question tests the chemistry of the link.

evidence.locator: Section 4. Storing Energy and Matter, Figure 4
evidence.supports: Producers combine sugar molecules into more complex molecules such as starch and cellulose; cellulose forms the rigid walls of plant cells.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 3.2 Carbohydrates
evidence.supports: Starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose; sugars join by a dehydration reaction that releases a water molecule; cellulose mostly makes up the plant cell wall; plants store starch in roots and seeds.

reviewFlags.issue: The Figure 4 caption (p. 50) says cellulose 'makes up the bulk of plant bodies'. Read as 'most of a plant', that overstates it: a living plant is mostly water, and even dry wood is only about 38 to 49 percent cellulose, with other cell-wall materials making up most of the rest. Cellulose is the largest single ingredient of wood, and cotton is nearly pure cellulose.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content calls cellulose the main material of plant cell walls and the largest single ingredient of wood (glossary, L04-Q21), and uses cotton as the nearly pure example. L04-Q20 says a cell wall is built mainly from cellulose. Evidence records quote the textbook's 'the bulk of plant bodies' instead of saying 'most'. No question asks what share of a plant is cellulose.

evidence.locator: Section 4. Storing Energy and Matter, Figure 4
evidence.supports: Simple sugars combine into starch and cellulose, and the caption says cellulose makes up the bulk of plant bodies.

evidence.title: Cell wall chemistry (Handbook of Wood Chemistry and Wood Composites)
evidence.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory (Rowell, Pettersen et al.)
evidence.supports: Cellulose makes up about 40 to 45 percent of softwood and 38 to 49 percent of hardwood.

evidence.title: Cotton fiber: a powerful single-cell model for cell wall and cellulose research
evidence.publisher: Frontiers in Plant Science (Haigler, Betancur, Stiff and Tuttle, 2012)
evidence.supports: A mature cotton fiber is more than 90 percent cellulose by weight.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 3.2 Carbohydrates
evidence.supports: Starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose, and cellulose mostly makes up the plant cell wall.

reviewFlags.issue: Figure 3 (p. 49) labels 'oxygen bubbles' on potted plants kept in air under glass jars, and the text says Ingenhousz collected and analyzed bubbles of gas. Gas bubbles form only on plants under water; in Figure 3 the 'bubbles' are drawn molecule symbols. Ingenhousz's own bubble observations used leaves plunged in jars of water.
reviewFlags.resolution: The O3 card describes leaves in jars of water gathering bubbles in sunshine, and its watchOut says the drawn bubbles are symbols. L04-Q13 and L04-Q14 keep the textbook's potted-plant setup but speak of oxygen given off, not bubbles. L04-Q17 states a water plant sealed in a jar of water. The O3 table row describes leaves in jars of water.

evidence.supports: Figure 3 shows potted plants under glass jars in light and in darkness, with 'oxygen bubbles' drawn as molecule callouts; the text says green parts produce oxygen only in light and that he collected and analyzed the gas bubbles.

evidence.title: Jan Ingenhousz, Experiments upon Vegetables (1779), excerpt
evidence.publisher: Le Moyne College, Classic Chemistry website (excerpt from Leicester and Klickstein, A Source Book in Chemistry 1400-1900)
evidence.supports: Ingenhousz plunged leaves into a clear jar filled with water and set it in the sunshine; bubbles of air gathered on the leaves in sunshine, hardly any formed after sunset, and leaves kept in shade gave air worse than common air.
